definition: Zenith means the highest point; the peak of success or power.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word zenith. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know zenith should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The newspaper hit its zenith in 1968, printing a million copies a day — a mark its sales never touched again.
An upswing is only a direction — things improving, with no claim about how high they sit; the zenith is a fixed point, the top itself.
A heyday is a stretch of flourishing years, and hidden inside it is the zenith: the single highest moment of the whole arc — above the zenith there is only sky, which is why the ladder stops here.

Prime is a stretch of peak strength — an athlete's prime lasts seasons; a city's prime can run a century. Zenith is a single point, the exact top of the arc, after which the only direction left is down. A prime is lived in; a zenith is touched once.

Zenith is a whole-word borrowing from Arabic astronomy, reshaped by a medieval copying error (samt misread as senit). Its root built no other English word, so there is no relative to spot — file it beside the sky it points to.
Zenith means the highest point; the peak of success or power.
For one decade the canal was the zenith of the young nation's fortunes: tolls filled the treasury, ports bloomed along its banks, and every map printed in Europe drew the waterway in gold.
The railroads ended all of it within a generation.
Zenith borrows its force from the sky: the astronomer's zenith is the point directly overhead, as high as anything can stand.
Applied to fortunes, it marks the exact top of the arc — with the quiet warning that whatever stands at its zenith has nowhere left to rise.
Zenith crowns eras and powers: an empire at its zenith, a career's zenith, the noon sun at zenith.
Its unit-mate pinnacle prefers a single crowning achievement, where zenith prefers the high point of a rise-and-fall story — historians' favorite, because it hints the fall is coming.
Its labelled opposite, the astronomer's nadir, marks the bottom of the same arc.

Sports writers still argue about the exact night of Ada Okafor's zenith.
Most point to the Lagos final of 2011: twenty-two years old, undefeated in fourteen months, she beat the world's number one in straight sets for the championship.
She played brilliantly for years afterward, but the record shows the arc bending: a lost title defense in 2013, semifinals by 2016, early rounds by the end of the decade.
Okafor herself is unsentimental about it.
'Every career is an arc,' she told an interviewer.
'One night you are at the top of yours.
You rarely know it at the time.' The Lagos scoresheet now hangs in the national museum, framed as the highest point of a rise no one has repeated since.
